title: POC scoping - Skyline AI - capacity & autoscale
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscaling strategy for Skyline AI's annotation and candidate-generation workloads. Discussed reserved GPUs for baseline throughput, burst capacity for peak traffic, fallback policies (model downgrade, queueing), and concrete benchmark plan and timeline. Agreed on pilot success criteria and next steps to run benchmarks in Redwood Dedicated environment with sample workload by 2026-07-23.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Carla Mendes (Redwood AE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Eve Torres (Head of ML, Skyline), Marcus Lin (Infra Lead, Skyline), Priya Rao (PM, Skyline)

[00:00] Carla: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Carla, AE on the account, Jonah is our SE who will drive the benchmark and capacity planning piece.
[00:20] Eve: Hi, Eve here. We're excited to scope the POC. We're mainly evaluating capacity / autoscale for two workloads: 1) annotation-assist (short prompts, 200-400 tokens) and 2) candidate gen / rerank (multi-turn, sometimes long contexts up to 2k).
[00:40] Marcus: Marcus, I'll be the infra contact. We care about predictable tail latency and cost control — also we have network peering and some VPC constraints.
[01:05] Jonah: Great. Can you give ballpark QPS and concurrency for each workload? That will shape reserved GPU sizing vs burst.
[01:20] Priya: For annotation-assist it's roughly 120 reqs/sec during working hours, peaks to ~220 qps for short bursts. Typical prompt ~256 tokens, generation ~120 tokens. For candidate-gen it's lower rps but heavier: around 15-25 reqs/sec, concurrent sessions up to 60, with sequence lengths sometimes 1.5k-2k tokens when we include history.
[01:55] Jonah: Nice detail, thanks. For the POC we usually start with a reserved baseline that covers steady-state, then configure burst capacity for peaks. Example: reserve capacity to handle 120 qps for annotation-assist, and be able to burst to ~250 qps with autoscale/burst. Do you have any hard latency SLOs?
[02:20] Eve: p95 for annotation should be under 350ms ideally. For candidate-gen p95 can be up to 1.2s given the long context, p99 we'd like under 2s. Error rate <1%.
[02:45] Jonah: That gives us clear targets. One wrinkle is batching — for short prompts we can batch across requests to improve throughput but it can bump tail latency if not tuned. We'll propose continuous batching with latency-aware cutoffs.
[03:10] Marcus: For cloud placement: we'll do Dedicated in our AWS VPC via peering. We prefer not to send PII to hosted. Also we need to validate KMS integration and audit logs.
[03:35] Carla: We'll include security docs and SOC2 attestation in the follow-up. For the POC topology, typical approach: reserve a small pool of GPUs (e.g., 2-4 A10/A100 equivalents) to cover steady-state, plus a burst pool of extra nodes that can be spun up quickly. Jonah, maybe you can sketch numbers?
[03:55] Jonah: Sure. Based on the numbers: annotation-assist at 120 qps with avg 120 token gen — assuming model similar to Llama-2-13B (quantized) on A10-like hardware, rough throughput per GPU is ~40-60 request/sec depending on batching and seq length. So baseline of 3 GPUs covers 120 qps with headroom. For burst to 250 qps I'd recommend an extra 3 GPUs (so total 6) as burst capacity. For candidate-gen, it'll require 1-2 heavier GPUs because the 2k context increases memory and reduces throughput; we can colocate workloads but better to partition pools.
[04:40] Eve: So you're recommending reserve 3 GPUs, burst to 6. What's the expected time to scale from reserve to burst? We need fast ramp for sudden load.
[04:55] Jonah: Our autoscale is hybrid: fast warm pool + cold pool. Warm pool is pre-warmed instances (or warmed models on GPUs) that can accept traffic within ~30-60 seconds. Cold pool provisioning (new instances) might take 2-4 minutes depending on cloud spin-up. We can configure a small warm burst (1-2 GPUs) to guarantee sub-60s spin up, and then allow autoscaler to add cold nodes for larger bursts.
[05:30] Marcus: What's the cost tradeoff for keeping warm GPUs? We want to minimize idle cost.
[05:40] Jonah: There's a cost vs latency trade. Warm GPUs incur a steady cost but give better tail latency. For the POC we typically recommend 1 warm extra GPU per service that needs <60s ramp. For example, baseline 3 reserved, 1 warm burst (always ready), and 2 cold burst nodes. That keeps cost moderate while meeting SLOs. We'll run cost sims in the follow-up.
[06:15] Priya: How do you handle fallback if burst capacity is exhausted or a region is degraded? We can't have requests failing silently.
[06:30] Carla: Good question — typical fallbacks: 1) route to a cheaper/smaller model variant with lower quality but fast latency, 2) apply request shaping (reduce max tokens or summarize prompt), 3) queue requests with informative retry-after headers, or 4) route to a secondary region or Dedicated fallback. Jonah can expand.
[06:55] Jonah: Yep. For Skyline I'd recommend a policy: primary is scale; secondary is degrade to a small-opt model variant for non-critical requests (e.g., internal annotation scoring), and for critical user-facing flows we queue with backpressure and surface a graceful degraded response. We can also keep a failover model pinned in another region if you need cross-region resilience.
[07:30] Marcus: From an infra POV we prefer model downgrade over cross-region because of latency. Also need to ensure KV cache behavior — if we route to smaller models, cache keys and prefixes might not be compatible.
[07:50] Jonah: Good point. We'll document cache compatibility and TTLs. For the POC we can disable cross-model KV reuse and only use prefix caching within each model to avoid incoherent results.
[08:10] Eve: For benchmarks, what will you run? Synthetic vs replay? We have traces.
[08:20] Jonah: Best is replay real traces with some synthetic spikes. Plan: Redwood will take your anonymized traces, run a replay against the Dedicated pool, measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, GPU utilization, and cost per 1k tokens. We'll also run stress tests to see autoscale behavior — ramp tests (sustained ramp over 5 min) and sudden spike tests.
[08:50] Marcus: We'll scrub and send traces by EOD tomorrow. Any infra credentials needed?
[09:00] Carla: We'll need an IAM role with read access for limited bench orchestration and VPC peering details. We'll send a template in the follow-up.
[09:12] Priya: Timeline? Can this POC be done in two weeks?
[09:20] Jonah: Typical POC timeline: Day 0-2: ingest traces + agree on scripts; Day 3-5: run baseline benchmarks; Day 6-9: tune batching, reserved sizing and warm pool; Day 10-12: run final stress tests and report. So ~10 business days is doable. For your dates, we could schedule the initial benchmark for 2026-07-23.
[09:50] Eve: That works. Success criteria recap: annotation-assist p95 <350ms, candidate-gen p95 <1.2s, error rate <1%, and cost per 1M tokens under a target we'll define after we see baseline.
[10:15] Jonah: We'll capture those as pass/fail. Also we'll include qualitative checks — hallucination/regression rate on a small eval set.
[10:30] Marcus: One more question: autoscale triggers and cooldowns — we have aggressive autoscaler thresholds that cause thrash. What's your recommendation?
[10:40] Jonah: We recommend multi-signal autoscaling: use a combination of queue length, GPU utilization, and observed p95 latency. Use conservative scale-down cooldowns (5-10 minutes) but faster scale-up policies. Also configure a cooldown for model loads that avoids killing newly-warmed nodes too fast. We'll share suggested thresholds.
[11:05] Priya: Are there any limitations we should know about — e.g., quantization compatibility, specific models that need more memory?
[11:15] Jonah: Yes — very large context + large models may need A100s with more VRAM; certain quantizations (4-bit) are fast but can affect quality. We'll include model-quantization tradeoff matrix in the deliverables.
[11:35] Carla: Ok, let's recap next steps. Redwood will share the architecture diagram, pricing, and a security pack by 2026-07-21. Jonah will prepare the benchmark harness and target tests; Marcus will provide traces and grant limited IAM/VPC details. We'll run the bench on 2026-07-23 and meet to review on 2026-07-27.
[11:55] Eve: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[12:05] Carla: Thanks, everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the doc links.

Notes: transcript contains some ASR noise (model names sometimes transcribed oddly, e.g., 'A one hundred' for A100), occasional speaker overlap.
